bib.title: FLASK: Fine-grained Language Model Evaluation based on Alignment Skill Sets

read.skipped: Reference list skimmed; radar-chart figures give axis labels only so per-skill figure values are not readable; Table 12 dataset rows read only partly.

question: Can LLM alignment be evaluated more reliably and interpretably by scoring each instruction on its own set of fine-grained skills instead of one overall preference score?
hypothesis: Fine-grained skill-level (and instance-level) scoring increases human-model correlation and reduces model-based evaluation bias.
contributions: FLASK: 12 skills in 4 primary abilities, plus domain and difficulty metadata annotated per instance
Skill-specific score rubrics for human and model evaluators, and instance-specific checklists for FLASK-HARD (89 instances)
Evidence that fine-grained rubrics raise human-model correlation and robustness to verbosity
Comparison of open-source and proprietary LLMs by skill, domain, difficulty and model size

method.summary: Instances (instruction + reference answer) are collected from NLP datasets; GPT-4 annotates the top-3 skills, a domain (of 10) and difficulty (1-5) per instance. An Eval LM (default GPT-4-0613) or human then writes a rationale and gives a 1-5 score per annotated skill using a handwritten per-skill rubric and the reference answer. FLASK-HARD adds LLM-generated, manually cleaned instance-specific subquestions.
method.task: fine-grained evaluation of instruction-following LLMs (LLM-as-judge with rubrics)

datasets.name: FLASK evaluation set
datasets.size: 1,740 instances from 122 datasets (Sec 3.2/Table 12); App J says 1,700 from 120
datasets.split: single-turn English, zero-shot; at most 20 instances per single-task dataset; inputs over 2048 length removed
datasets.source: Collected by authors from NLP datasets (MMLU, BBH, GSM8K, Self-Instruct, WizardLM, Koala, Vicuna, etc.); missing reference answers filled by the Eval LM
datasets.preprocessing: instructions manually written for datasets lacking them

datasets.name: FLASK-HARD
datasets.preprocessing: Eval LM generates at most 5 subquestions per instance; duplicates and skill-unrelated ones removed manually

datasets.name: Human-evaluation subset
datasets.split: random sample of the FLASK set
datasets.source: 10 labelers from KAIST, 3 labelers per instance (60 instances each)

other.use: default Eval LM; also metadata annotator

models.name: Vicuna 7B/13B/33B, Alpaca 13B, WizardLM 13B, Tulu 7B/13B/30B/65B, Llama2 Chat 13B/70B, StableVicuna 13B, GPT4-Alpaca 13B, SelFee 13B

inference.decoding: target-model response generation at temperature 0.7, max generation length 1024
inference.temperature: 0.7 for target models; Eval LM temperature not stated except 1.0 for the agreement runs
inference.samples: 1 grader run per response for main results (inferred: not stated); 3 runs at temperature 1.0 for model-model agreement
inference.prompting: Eval LM sees instruction, reference answer, response, skill rubric(s); must write feedback per skill before score, then return a Python dict skill->score; skill order of descriptions shuffled for metadata annotation

parameters.skills_excluded_in_size_analysis: Completeness and Conciseness excluded in the model-comparison analysis (length-dependent)

other.skill_agnostic_baseline: reference-guided single-answer grading prompt in the style of Zheng et al. 2023, one 1-5 score, copied to all skills for correlation
other.human_labelers: also gave domain/skill acceptance and N/A when the skill was irrelevant

metrics.name: Spearman rho, Kendall tau, Pearson r between human and model scores
metrics.definition: computed over per-skill scores on the 200-instance human subset

metrics.name: Krippendorff's alpha
metrics.definition: agreement among 3 human labelers (H-H), 3 GPT-4 runs at T=1.0 (M-M); H-M is Pearson human vs model

metrics.name: Robustness to verbosity
metrics.definition: ratio of cases where the Eval LM gives the same score to original and verbose-rewritten GPT-3.5 response on FLASK-HARD

metrics.name: Mean skill score
metrics.definition: mean 1-5 score per skill, aggregated by skill, domain, difficulty

eval.protocol: Human and GPT-4 scoring on 200 instances and 4 models; ablations of reference answer, rationale and rubric; no significance tests or confidence intervals reported.

prompts.text: We would like to request your feedback on the performance of the response of the assistant to the user instruction displayed below. In the feedback, I want you to rate the quality of the response in these 3 categories according to each score rubric: {skill description rubric} [Instruction] {question} [Ground truth Answer] {ground truth answer} [Assistant's Response] {answer} [The End of Assistant's Response] Please give feedback on the assistant's responses. Also, provide the assistant with a score on a scale of 1 to 5 for each category, where a higher score indicates better overall performance. Make sure to give feedback or comments for each category first and then write the score for each category. Only write the feedback corresponding to the score rubric for each category. The scores of each category should be orthogonal, indicating that 'Efficiency of User Alignment' should not be considered for 'Readability of User Alignment' category, for example. Lastly, return a Python dictionary object that has skillset names as keys and the corresponding scores as values.

Score 1: The response totally fails to accomplish the requirements of the subquestion. Score 2: partially satisfies ... needs major challenges and improvements. Score 3: mainly satisfies ... lacks some parts compared to the ground truth answer. Score 4: satisfies ... competitive to the ground truth answer. Score 5: fully satisfies ... better than the ground truth answer. [Subquestions] {subquestions} [Instruction] {question} [Ground truth Answer] {ground truth answer} [Assistant's Response] {answer} ... give feedback for each subquestion first, then score; subquestions are orthogonal; return a Python dictionary with subquestion index as keys and scores as values. (abridged)

Please act as an impartial judge and evaluate the quality of the response provided by an AI assistant to the user question displayed below. Your evaluation should consider factors such as the helpfulness, relevance, accuracy, depth, creativity, and level of detail of the response. Begin your evaluation by providing a short explanation. Be as objective as possible. After providing your explanation, please rate the response on a scale of 1 to 5 by strictly following this format: "[[rating]]", for example: "Rating: [[5]]". [Question] {question} [Ground Truth Answer] {ground truth answer} [The Start of Assistant's Answer] {answer} [The End of Assistant's Answer]

prompts.purpose: Difficulty annotation (general; separate Math and Coding versions)
prompts.text: We would like you to label the difficulty of the following question. You should classify the knowledge needed to solve the question into simple lifestyle knowledge, advanced lifestyle knowledge, formal education knowledge, major level knowledge, and expert level knowledge. You must write only one class without any explanation. (plus level descriptions and one example each)

results.claim: GPT-4 grader with skill-specific rubric (FLASK) correlates with human scores more than skill-agnostic reference-guided scoring (Spearman).
results.setup: 200 FLASK instances sampled randomly, 4 target models (GPT-3.5, Bard, Vicuna-13B, Alpaca-13B), human labels from 10 labelers (3 per instance) vs Eval LM scores; correlation between human and model scores per skill-annotation
results.note: Skill-agnostic (GPT-4) row: rho 0.641, tau 0.495, r 0.673. FLASK (GPT-4): rho 0.680, tau 0.541, r 0.732. For the skill-agnostic setting a uniform score is assigned to every skill (footnote 6).

limits: Human study is small: 200 instances, 10 labelers (3 per instance), 4 models; authors concede labeler pool and set should be larger and more diverse (App A.1).
Human agreement is only moderate (alpha 0.488) with central tendency bias and fatigue; Readability alpha 0.089 means that skill's human reference is nearly noise.
Instance-specific rubrics were validated only through a verbosity-robustness test, not against human judgments, and applied only to FLASK-HARD (89 instances, outlier-prone).
Only the GPT-4 grader results are strong; with GPT-3.5 Pearson is unchanged by skill-specific rubrics (0.450 vs 0.449).
Reference answers matter most (largest ablation drop) and missing ones were generated by the Eval LM itself, so the grader partly grades against its own answers.
Single-turn, English, zero-shot, text only; GPT-4 grader known to favour its own style and long responses; Completeness correlates 0.737 with length.
Dataset counts are internally inconsistent (1,740/122 vs 1,700/120); FLASK-HARD 89 vs 170 Level-5 instances in the whole set.
No confidence intervals or significance tests for the correlation differences; model versions are mid-2023 API snapshots (dated).
